vignette:
Amina, a 42-year-old divorced factory worker who had emigrated from East Africa years earlier, described the event that changed her life as happening in a room that was too small to breathe in. During the torture, she had been held close enough to smell sweat, metal, and a sharp chemical odor she could still not name without flinching; she said the details were so extreme that the memory felt unreal, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. Even now, when she tried to tell it, it came back in fragments that felt alien and hard to believe had happened to her body at all. What made the memory more dangerous was how easily it could return in the present: the smell of a damp hallway, a particular body odor, or the sight of a uniform sleeve could pull it back with force, and during those moments she would feel her body react before she had time to think. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that belief had sharpened after the torture into the conviction that she could no longer trust her own body or do the things that had once defined her, including moving confidently through work and home.

In the months after she was released, Amina began arranging her life around anything that might remind her of that room. She stopped wearing the kinds of clothes she had worn then, because a similar fabric or cut could make her stomach tighten and send her back into the memory. In the morning she put on heavy make-up, not out of vanity but to feel less recognizable and less exposed, as though it could help her hide from whatever might be watching. She kept her mind occupied all the time, filling every spare minute with noise, chores, and television so there would be no empty space for the memory to enter. At work on the factory floor, where other workers moved close to one another around the machines, physical proximity was enough to set her on edge; if someone stood too near or reached past her, she found herself tensing and drifting away from the task, then trying to pull herself back by forcing her attention elsewhere. The smell of the hot machinery during humid weather could catch her too, especially on days when the weather felt like the season of the assault, and that familiar heat could make her think of the event before she had even realized she was remembering. Hearing related names also unsettled her; if someone mentioned a name that sounded like one she associated with the men involved, she would go silent and work harder at distraction, because she feared her own reactions would betray her.

Amina’s sense that the world was dangerous fed this constant vigilance. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, often stopping in the middle of ordinary tasks to check the door and the hallway, and she startled badly at small noises that would not bother most people. What frightened her most was how quickly her body seemed to know danger; the instant she heard an unexpected knock or a footstep outside her apartment, she felt her heart race and her muscles brace before she could tell herself she was safe. Those moments also pushed her back into the memory, because the same bodily alarm would bring with it the smell, the helplessness, and the sense that the torture was happening again. Then she would think, with growing certainty, that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her, and that weakness made her even more convinced that the world remained dangerous. As that fear settled in, she became even more likely to choose routes, clothes, and routines that might keep reminders away from her.

Over time, the effort to stay ahead of the memory made the memory more present. The more Amina kept herself occupied and avoided similar clothes, the more any interruption in that routine stood out as threatening, and the more sharply the torture returned when it did break through. A stray odor at work or the close placement of another worker could bring back the strange, unreal feeling of the event, followed by the sense that it was happening to someone else and yet inside her own body. Once the memory returned, she would scan the room, listen for intruders, and jump at ordinary sounds, which made her more certain that danger was near. That alarm in turn made her negative beliefs feel truer: if her body reacted so strongly, then she could not trust it, and if she could not trust it, she must be living in a world that was still unsafe. She arrived for help only after her avoidance and hypervigilance had begun to cost her at work and at home, and after her ex-husband and sister urged her to speak to someone when she admitted she was exhausted from never letting her mind rest. What she hoped for was simple and frightening at the same time: to feel safe enough to sleep without listening for the door, and to believe that her body and her life could belong to her again.
